title: Multi-Node LLM Inference: From One Node to N
description: Scaling LLM inference serving from one 8-GPU node to N nodes: replication and routing, prefill/decode disaggregation, cross-node MoE, multi-node KV management, and the open-source serving stack.

parts.title: The Multi-Node Frame

modules.title: Interconnect and Transport: The Physical Layer of Multi-Node Serving
modules.description: The bandwidth/latency ladder from NVLink inside a node to InfiniBand/RoCE between nodes to the NVL72 fabric, and what GPUDirect RDMA and UCX/NIXL actually move.

After this module Aman can compute, given a payload size and an interconnect, how long a cross-node operation takes.

modules.title: Replication and Routing: KV-Cache-Aware, Prefix-Aware, and SLO-Aware Request Placement
modules.description: Why naive round-robin fails once every replica carries different KV-cache state, and the mechanisms -- approximate hashing vs. precise event-streaming -- routers use to learn and score that state.
modules.scope: In: the replication model (N independent TP8 engine copies, each with private KV cache) and why request placement stops being stateless; prefix-cache-aware scoring (block hashing, rolling hash chains, LRU indexes); precise KV-cache indexing via KVEvents emitted over ZeroMQ; session affinity vs. prefix affinity; load- and SLO-aware scoring layered on prefix affinity; the layered filter -> score -> select pipeline as implemented by llm-d's scheduler and the Gateway API Inference Extension's EPP contract; sglang-router and vLLM production-stack's simpler router designs as points of comparison. modules.title: Why Disaggregation Pays: Goodput, Interference, and the Ratio Decision
modules.description: The queueing-theoretic and empirical case for splitting prefill and decode into separate pools, the interference mechanism that motivates it, and the TCO crossover point where it stops paying.

modules.title: Prefix Caching and Tiered KV Offload Across Nodes: Mooncake's Architecture
modules.description: The KVCache-centric view of a serving cluster -- HBM to host DRAM to SSD to remote, addressed by content hash -- and Mooncake, the paper and system that made this architecture concrete.

Heterogeneous TP with GPU staging buffer: 2-5x throughput gain when prefill/decode use different TP sizes; incompatible with MLA models
Failure detection specifics: SGLANG_DISAGGREGATION_HEARTBEAT_INTERVAL (5.0s default), bootstrap handshake timeout (300s default)
sglang-router: standalone Rust load balancer, PD-aware routing algorithms, versioning (0.3.2)
Comparing SGLang's framing to DistServe/Mooncake's interference argument (Module 3): same conclusion, different diagnosis
SGL-JAX as the bridge extending this stack to TPU, previewed here and fully treated in Module 18

modules.title: TensorRT-LLM and Triton: Disaggregated Serving on GB200
modules.description: TensorRT-LLM's context/generation server terminology, its cache-transceiver mechanism, and the disaggregation speedup numbers NVIDIA measured across models and GPU counts on GB200.
modules.scope: In: TensorRT-LLM's own terminology (context servers = prefill, generation servers = decode); the cache-transceiver mechanism (KvCacheTransceiverV2, default NIXL backend, TRTLLM_NIXL_KVCACHE_BACKEND selecting UCX/LIBFABRIC, transport over RDMA/NVLink); the disagg_request_id binding mechanism (TensorRT-LLM specifics, general pattern already in Module 4); measured speedups across models and configurations on GB200 (DeepSeek R1 with/without MTP, Qwen3, by ISL:OSL ratio, by GPU count 4-32); dynamic node joining/leaving as explicitly in-progress, not-GA; Triton's role as the serving frontend TensorRT-LLM backends into. Out: general PD mechanics (Module 4); wide-EP mechanism (Module 5). After this module Aman can read TensorRT-LLM's disaggregation benchmarks critically, knowing which speedup numbers apply to which workload shape.
topics: Terminology: context servers (prefill) vs. generation servers (decode)
Cache-transceiver mechanism: KvCacheTransceiverV2, default NIXL backend, TRTLLM_NIXL_KVCACHE_BACKEND (UCX default vs. LIBFABRIC)
disagg_request_id: why context and generation phases of one request must share a single ID
Communication protocols supported: MPI, UCX, NIXL, over RDMA/NVLink
Measured speedups on GB200 by workload: DeepSeek R1 (1.4x-1.8x without MTP, 1.6x-2.5x with MTP), Qwen3 (1.7x-6.11x), by GPU count (4-32 per instance)
Why speedup varies 1.4x-6.11x by ISL:OSL ratio and model: reading these numbers as workload-shape-dependent, not hardware constants
Dynamic node joining/leaving: explicitly in progress, being built on top of the existing cache-transceiver mechanism, not yet GA
Triton as the serving frontend TensorRT-LLM plugs into

parts.title: Operations, Economics, and the Frontier

modules.title: Kubernetes Deployment Topologies and Operations at Fleet Scale
modules.description: How a multi-node inference fleet is actually deployed and operated -- LeaderWorkerSet as the multi-host replication primitive, SLO-driven autoscaling, multi-tenant serving, observability, and upgrade/failure handling.
modules.scope: In: LeaderWorkerSet (LWS) as the Kubernetes API for deploying a sharded multi-host unit of replication, and its co-design with llm-d; concrete parallelism-to-GPU-count topology examples (KServe's tensorParallelSize x pipelineParallelSize = total GPUs, 16-GPU/2-node worked example); the orchestration layer landscape (Ray Serve LLM's multi-node/multi-model primitives, KServe's multinode ServingRuntime, AIBrix's component set) and where each fits relative to Dynamo/llm-d; multi-model and multi-tenant serving patterns; observability -- what metrics actually matter for a multi-node fleet vs. vanity metrics; upgrade and failure handling (rolling upgrades of stateful multi-host pods, GPU hardware-failure detection, drain-before-remove). Out: the SLO-autoscaling algorithm internals already covered for Dynamo's Planner (Module 9, cross-referenced); capacity-planning arithmetic (Module 15). After this module Aman can specify a concrete Kubernetes topology for an N-node deployment and knows which orchestration layer fits which operational need.
topics: LeaderWorkerSet: deploying a group of pods as one unit of replication for multi-host sharded inference; co-design with llm-d
KServe's parallelism arithmetic: tensorParallelSize x pipelineParallelSize = total GPUs, worked 16-GPU/2-node example

Orchestration layer landscape: Ray Serve LLM (multi-node/multi-model, LLMConfig/build_openai_app/serve.run), KServe multinode ServingRuntime, AIBrix (Gateway/Routing, App-Tailored Autoscaler, Distributed KV Cache, GPU Hardware Failure Detection)
Where each orchestration layer sits relative to Dynamo/llm-d: complementary Kubernetes control-plane vs. inference-specific orchestration
Multi-model and multi-tenant serving patterns: shared InferencePool across models, LoRA-adapter routing by model name
Observability that matters: TTFT/ITL percentiles, KV-cache utilization, per-pool queue depth, GPU power/utilization, vs. metrics that don't move the needle
Upgrade handling: rolling upgrade of stateful multi-host sharded pods, drain-before-remove pattern cross-referenced against Module 4's xPyD
GPU hardware-failure detection and recovery at fleet scale, using AIBrix's dedicated component as a concrete example

modules.title: Capacity Planning and Economics: Goodput, Tokens/s/$, and Little's-Law Reasoning at Rack Scale
modules.description: The arithmetic for sizing a multi-node deployment from published numbers -- goodput under TTFT/ITL SLOs, tokens/s/$ as a function of N, and queueing-theoretic reasoning about when adding nodes stops helping.
modules.scope: In: precise metric definitions (TTFT, TPOT/ITL formulas including the N-request averaging subtlety, goodput = %requests meeting all SLOs); the single-node batch-size/latency/throughput baseline planners must know before scaling (14x throughput for 4x latency at batch 64; continuous batching's 10-20x gain; the sublinear GPU-count-to-latency relationship at low batch size); scaling tokens/s/$ with N using DeepSeek's and SGLang's published cost numbers as worked examples; TCO-per-million-tokens as the correct optimization target (InferenceMAX framing, cross-referenced from Module 3) applied as a planning tool; queueing-theoretic capacity reasoning grounded in DistServe's M/D/1 analysis rather than unsourced blog heuristics, explicitly flagging why an unsourced Little's-Law blog claim was excluded from this course. Out: the disaggregation pay-off decision itself (Module 3, already made); per-project economics (Modules 6, 9-13, cross-referenced for worked numbers). After this module Aman can size a deployment -- node count, pool split, expected tokens/s/$ -- from a target SLO and a published per-node throughput number.
topics: Precise metric definitions: TTFT, TPOT (1-request formula and N-request averaging subtlety, Avg TPOT vs. Avg ITL divergence), goodput
Single-node batch-size/latency/throughput baseline: 4x latency for 14x throughput at batch 64; continuous batching's 10-20x gain over static/dynamic batching
Why doubling GPU count doesn't halve latency at low batch size (0.7x latency at 4->8 GPUs, Llama2-70B): the capacity-planning trap of assuming linear scaling
Scaling tokens/s/$ with N: worked economics from DeepSeek's own numbers ($87,072/day cost, 545% margin) and SGLang's reproduction ($0.20/1M output tokens)
TCO-per-million-tokens as optimization target and the interactivity-dependent crossover, cross-referenced from Module 3's ~90 tok/s/user finding, applied as a sizing decision tool
Queueing-theoretic capacity reasoning: DistServe's M/D/1 goodput analysis as the grounded alternative to informal Little's-Law heuristics
Why an unsourced Little's-Law blog claim (30-70% throughput from work-conserving schedulers) was excluded, and what to use instead
Worked sizing structure: given a target TTFT/ITL SLO and a per-node throughput number, derive required node count and expected cost per million tokens
disagreements: When does prefill/decode disaggregation actually pay off?

modules.title: The Research Frontier: Live Migration, Fused Megakernels, and What Is Still Unsettled
modules.description: What the open-source stack has not yet productionized -- cross-instance live request migration, kernel-fusion alternatives to orchestration complexity -- and where the field's own published numbers still disagree.
modules.scope: In: Llumnix's cross-instance live-migration mechanism (near-zero-downtime, sequence-length-independent; unifying load balancing, de-fragmentation, prioritization, and autoscaling under one 'virtual usage' abstraction) as a capability that is research-proven but not yet part of the mainstream production stack surveyed in Part 5; Stanford Hazy Research/Scaling Intelligence Lab's kernel-fusion line of work as a contrasting research direction -- Tokasaurus (dynamic Hydragen grouping, adaptive CPU/GPU pipelining) and ThunderMLA (fused decode megakernel via a GPU-resident virtual instruction set, 20-35% faster than FlashMLA) built on ThunderKittens, explicitly correcting the 'Thunder Agent' misnomer, which does not name a real project; synthesis of this course's open disagreements as unresolved as of 2026-09-17: the EP320-vs-EP144 DeepSeek discrepancy, TensorRT-LLM's not-yet-GA dynamic node joining/leaving, and the disaggregation-pays-off conditionality. Out: no new mechanism categories -- this module is explicitly synthesis plus two research lines not covered elsewhere. After this module Aman knows what a state-of-the-art multi-node deployment does not yet do, and which of this course's numbers are most likely to be stale within a year.
topics: Llumnix's live migration mechanism: near-zero-downtime, constant-in-sequence-length migration between running instances
The 'virtual usage' abstraction unifying four rescheduling purposes: load balancing, de-fragmentation, prioritization, autoscaling
Llumnix's measured gains (15x P99 TTFT, 2x P99 per-token latency vs. INFaaS on 16 GPUs; 36% cost saving) and why this capability is absent from Part 5's production stacks
Tokasaurus: dynamic Hydragen grouping for shared prefixes, pipeline parallelism for NVLink-less GPUs, async TP for NVLink GPUs -- a throughput-first alternative to disaggregation-first design
ThunderMLA: the fused 'megakernel' concept -- a GPU-resident virtual instruction set eliminating kernel-launch overhead, 20-35% faster than DeepSeek's own FlashMLA
ThunderKittens as the underlying tile-kernel DSL that makes megakernel fusion tractable (naming correction: not 'Thunder Agent', which does not exist)
Open disagreement recap: EP320 (Dec 2024) vs. EP144 (Feb 2025) for DeepSeek decode -- genuine deployment evolution, not error
Open disagreement recap: TensorRT-LLM's dynamic node joining/leaving explicitly in progress, not GA -- what production readiness would require

Open disagreement recap: disaggregation's pay-off conditionality -- near-unconditional goodput win (DistServe/Mooncake) vs. interactivity-conditional TCO win (InferenceMAX) -- and why both are correct under their own metric
What is most likely to be stale within a year: NIXL/Dynamo's monthly-cadence version churn, EP configurations, the TCO crossover point as newer hardware ships

modules.title: AMD MI300X/MI355X Multi-Node Serving: RCCL, InfiniBand/RoCE, and vLLM-ROCm
modules.description: What transfers from the NVIDIA-centric stack to AMD's Instinct platform and what does not -- RCCL's IB/RoCE setup, MI300X/MI355X's interconnect numbers, and vLLM-ROCm's DP+EP results.
modules.scope: In: MI300X architecture numbers (192GB HBM3 @ 5.2TB/s, 4th-gen Infinity Fabric 896GB/s/GPU, 8-GPU platform aggregate 1.5TB HBM3 @ 42.4TB/s vs. H100 HGX's 640GB @ 25.6TB/s); MI355X's generational jump (288GB HBM3e @ 8TB/s, 5th-gen Infinity Fabric 538GB/s/chip, RoCEv2 via Pollara 400GbE NIC); RCCL multi-node setup mechanics (required RDMA packages, MASTER_ADDR/NNODES/NODE_RANK, NCCL_SOCKET_IFNAME, NCCL_IB_HCA, NCCL_IB_GID_INDEX=3 for RoCE, automatic RDMA activation on InfiniBand vs. exact-version RoCE library matching); vLLM-ROCm's state (AITER attention backends, MoRIIOConnector as the ROCm-specific disaggregation connector already named in Module 11, DP+EP throughput gains 16-47% over TP at high concurrency, 7,114 TPS DeepSeek-R1 at 1024 concurrent requests); InferenceMAX's MI300X-vs-MI355X per-MW comparison. Out: re-deriving PD/EP/routing mechanisms already covered generically (Modules 2-6) -- here only what is AMD-specific or numerically different. After this module Aman knows exactly which multi-node mechanisms in this course port to AMD unchanged and which are AMD-specific substitutions.
topics: MI300X spec numbers: 192GB HBM3 @ 5.2TB/s, 304 CUs/1,216 Matrix Cores, 4th-gen Infinity Fabric 896GB/s/GPU
8-GPU MI300X platform vs. 8-GPU H100 HGX: 1.5TB @ 42.4TB/s vs. 640GB @ 25.6TB/s, the memory-capacity case for large MoE inference
MI355X generational jump: 288GB HBM3e @ 8TB/s, 5th-gen Infinity Fabric 538GB/s/chip (~4.3TB/s aggregate per node), 1,400W TDP/chip
Multi-node fabric: RoCEv2 Ethernet via Pollara 400GbE NIC as the standard scale-out path, vs. NVIDIA's IB-first default
RCCL multi-node setup: required RDMA packages, MASTER_ADDR/NNODES/NODE_RANK launch variables, NCCL_SOCKET_IFNAME, NCCL_IB_HCA
RoCE-specific requirement: NCCL_IB_GID_INDEX=3 and exact RoCE-library-version matching across hosts, vs. InfiniBand's automatic RDMA activation
vLLM-ROCm's AITER attention backends: 2.7-4.4x TPS over legacy ROCM_ATTN, 1.2-1.5x over TRITON_MLA for MLA models
DP+EP on ROCm: 16-47% throughput gain over TP at >=512 concurrent requests, 7,114 TPS DeepSeek-R1 at 1024 concurrent requests
MoRIIOConnector as the ROCm-specific KV-disaggregation connector, cross-referenced against Module 11's connector list
InferenceMAX's per-provisioned-MW comparison: MI300X 750k tok/s/MW vs. MI355X 2.55M tok/s/MW at 90 tok/s/user interactivity

modules.title: TPU Multi-Host Serving: ICI, Pathways, and JetStream
modules.description: The TPU-native alternative to the GPU stack's node/fabric model -- ICI mesh topology, single-controller Pathways orchestration, and JetStream as the serving engine -- contrasted mechanism by mechanism against Parts 1-6.
modules.scope: In: TPU generation specs (v6e: 256-chip pod, 800GBps bidirectional ICI/chip, 32GB HBM/chip @ 1638GBps, 8-chip single-VM inference-optimized slice; TPU7x/Ironwood: 9,216-chip pod, 1,200GBps ICI/chip, 192GB HBM/chip @ ~7.37TB/s) and how ICI's mesh/torus topology differs structurally from NVLink's switched fabric and IB's fat-tree; the single-controller Pathways model (pathways-proxy, pathways-rm, jax-tpu, jetstream-http) as the orchestration analog to Dynamo/llm-d, built on the same LeaderWorkerSet primitive; JetStream as the throughput/memory-optimized serving engine (JAX/MaxText and PyTorch reference implementations); multi-host slice topology examples (v6e-16, disaggregated-mode two-v6e-8 example) and what disaggregation means when the fabric is already a single low-latency mesh; checkpoint-restoration timings as an operational reality GPU-stack modules don't surface; the access-model caveat (Pathways not fully self-serve GA); SGLang's SGL-JAX bridge as the point where the GPU-centric open-source router/PD/wide-EP stack is being ported onto this substrate. Out: re-deriving routing/PD/EP mechanisms already covered -- here only what changes when ICI replaces NVLink/IB and Pathways replaces Dynamo/llm-d. After this module Aman can map every mechanism in this course onto its TPU-side equivalent or absence.
topics: TPU v6e pod spec: 256 chips, 800GBps bidirectional ICI/chip, 32GB HBM/chip @ 1638GBps, 2D torus topology

Operational realities: checkpoint restoration timing (7 min for Llama3.1-405B, 2 min for Llama2-70B) as a cost GPU-stack modules don't surface
